extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal financial assistance (K-12 and higher education institutions), school administrators, and legal practitioners advising on Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how §106.31(a)(2) (de minimis harm and participation consistent with gender identity) applies to education programs and activities, who is covered, applicable exceptions, and related implementation issues (facilities, athletics, documentation, privacy, and First Amendment considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective de minimis-harm standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm under §106.31(a)(2) must be genuine and objectively non-trivial and assessed from the perspective of a reasonable person in the individual's position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective standard is consistent with longstanding anti-discrimination law and judicially administrable (see Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co.). It avoids reliance on an individual's unusual subjective feelings. The regulation need not elaborate further because the standard is grounded in established legal doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of persons covered
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) applies to any 'person,' including students, employees, applicants for admission or employment, parents, visiting lecturers, community members invited to campus, and others participating or attempting to participate in a recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is not limited to students; it covers any individual interacting with the recipient's programs or activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to permissible sex separation/differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) applies to circumstances in which a recipient engages in permissible sex separation or differentiation (e.g., restrooms and locker rooms under §106.33, access to classes and activities under §106.34(a)-(b), and appearance codes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in contexts where sex separation is generally permitted, recipients must carry out separation consistent with Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate and avoid causing more than de minimis harm unless an exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory exceptions where more-than-de-minimis harm may be permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on causing more than de minimis harm does not apply 'except as permitted by 20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(1) through (9) and the corresponding regulations at §§106.12 through 106.15, 20 U.S.C. 1686 and its corresponding regulation §106.32(b)(1), or §106.41(b)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated statutory exceptions (religious exemption, military/merchant marine institutions, membership practices of certain organizations, admissions exceptions, living facilities under 20 U.S.C. 1686, sex-separate athletic teams under §106.41(b), etc.) are the limited contexts in which Title IX or its implementing regs may permit what would otherwise be more than de minimis harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Athletics exception and program‑wide evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) does not apply to male and female athletic teams a recipient offers under §106.41(b); athletics have long been evaluated program-wide rather than at the individual level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with the Javits Amendment and longstanding regulations, exclusion from a particular team on the basis of sex may impose more than de minimis harm on an individual but still be permissible if equal athletic opportunity is provided program-wide (see §§106.41(b),(c)). The Department plans separate rulemaking on sport-related eligibility criteria; categorical bans on transgender participation would not satisfy the proposed standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from hostile-environment standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The hostile-environment standard in the definition of 'sex-based harassment' (§106.2) applies to determining whether harassing conduct rises to a hostile environment; §106.31(a)(2) is different and addresses how a recipient carries out otherwise permissible different treatment or separation on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients' obligations to respond to sex-based harassment are described in §106.44(a); do not conflate hostile-environment analysis with the de minimis-harm rule governing sex-based separation/treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation consistent with gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must not prevent a person from participating in an education program or activity consistent with the person's gender identity when that person seeks to do so, unless an applicable statutory/regulatory exception permits otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection applies across contexts (except the enumerated exceptions), including access to facilities and classes; it is not limited to transgender students and is intended to prevent sex-based harms caused by exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining gender identity—permissible evidentiary practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many recipients rely on a student's consistent assertion or on written confirmation by the student or the student's parent, counselor, coach, or teacher to determine gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may not require invasive medical inquiries or burdensome documentation (such as amended birth certificates or evidence of medical treatment) to validate gender identity for purposes of §106.31(a)(2), and they may not require documentation when such access is prohibited by law in the jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonbinary students and individualized accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) does not prescribe an approach for nonbinary students; a recipient may coordinate with the student (and parents as appropriate) to determine how best to provide safe and nondiscriminatory access to facilities and programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options may include use of gender-neutral or single-occupancy facilities or other tailored arrangements; recipients must ensure access that does not cause more than de minimis harm and must respond promptly and effectively when they know of conduct that may constitute sex discrimination (§106.44(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted voluntary accommodations vs. mandatory segregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations prohibits a recipient from offering single-occupancy, gender-neutral, or other private alternatives to any students who seek additional privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While voluntary private accommodations are allowed, requiring a student to use a separate facility can be stigmatizing and may impose more than de minimis harm; recipients should avoid mandatory segregation that singles out or stigmatizes protected individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and privacy concerns must be addressed without categorical exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have a legitimate interest in protecting all students' safety and privacy, but generalized or unsubstantiated claims that transgender students pose a safety risk do not justify excluding them from sex-separate spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly rejected claims that a transgender person's mere presence in a sex-separated space constitutes a privacy or safety violation (cases cited: Grimm, Whitaker, Boyertown, Parents for Priv., Cruzan). Recipients can adopt and enforce neutral rules that protect privacy/safety without excluding students based on gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional limits on regulation—First Amendment and due process
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) does not limit §106.6(d): nothing in Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict rights protected by the First Amendment or deprive constitutional protections under the Due Process Clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must not invoke Title IX to restrict speech, expression, or other constitutional rights; the Department will implement and enforce regulations consistent with constitutional guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approach to appearance codes and other policies
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) applies to policies such as appearance codes (dress and grooming) and requires that such policies be applied without causing more than de minimis harm on the basis of sex or gender identity, except where statute/regulations permit otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will interpret 'sex' in the context of these policies consistent with Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate and relevant case law; recipients should avoid policies that treat individuals inconsistenly with their gender identity in ways that cause more than de minimis harm.
